hops.title: Isl1 works in the pancreas, the heart and the spinal cord
hops.text: Isl1, also called Islet-1, was identified in 1990 as a protein that binds part of a rat insulin gene enhancer, and that first report found it mainly in pancreatic endocrine cells. It also helps build the heart, marking cardiac progenitors and a subset of pacemaker cells. In 2023 a team compared human stem cells heading toward heart cells with stem cells heading toward motor neurons. In cardiac progenitors, Isl1 shares most of its DNA sites with a cardiac partner, NKX2.5. Force NKX2.5 into motor neuron progenitors and Isl1 picks up a subset of those cardiac sites. Different partners, different DNA.

sources.citation: Karlsson O, Thor S, Norberg T, Ohlsson H, Edlund T. Insulin gene enhancer binding protein Isl-1 is a member of a novel class of proteins containing both a homeo- and a Cys-His domain. Nature 344:879-882 (1990)
Sun Y et al. Islet 1 is expressed in distinct cardiovascular lineages, including pacemaker and coronary vascular cells. Developmental Biology 304:286-296 (2007)
Maven BEJ et al. ISL1 genomic occupancy and partner factors in human cardiac progenitors and motor neuron progenitors. Stem Cell Reports (2023), PMID 37863045

hops.title: The chick sufficiency test ends with Scotch tape
hops.text: Electroporating a chick neural tube sounds like high-tech surgery, and then the recipe calls for household tape. Biologists cut a small window in the shell of a fertilized hen's egg, inject plasmid DNA into the hollow neural tube, and deliver five square pulses at twenty-five volts, each lasting twenty-five milliseconds. DNA moves toward the positive electrode, so mostly one side of the tube takes up the added gene. The window then gets taped shut and the egg goes back into the incubator; one chick forebrain protocol recommends reinforcing that seal with Scotch tape.

sources.citation: Nakamura H, Funahashi J. Introduction of DNA into chick embryos by in ovo electroporation. Methods 24:43-48 (2001)
Cardenas A, Borrell V. In ovo electroporation of embryonic chick and snake brains. STAR Protocols 2:100692 (2021), steps 15-16

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A speckled brown chicken egg in a cardboard cup on a wooden bench, a strip of clear tape patched over its shell, small scissors beside it.
image.caption: After electric pulses drive injected DNA into chick neural tube cells, researchers tape the eggshell shut and keep incubating.

hops.afterHeading: Which motor neuron: Hox proteins and FoxP1 along the cord
hops.title: Walking circuits did not wait for legs
hops.text: Researchers had proposed that some spinal circuits coordinating limb movements arose as vertebrates moved onto land. The little skate, Leucoraja erinacea, a flat relative of sharks whose common ancestor with tetrapods lived at least 439 million years ago, complicates that timeline. Two weeks after hatching, these skates walk along a submerged surface on their pelvic fins, alternating left and right as a tetrapod does. They wire those fins with a version of the Hox and FoxP1 program that organizes your limb motor neurons. Little skates also lack the entire HoxC cluster, and their FoxP1-positive motor neurons form one continuous column from pectoral to pelvic fin levels.

sources.citation: Jung H et al. The ancient origins of neural substrates for land walking. Cell 172:667-682 (2018)
Andreev PS et al. Spiny chondrichthyan from the lower Silurian of South China. Nature 609:969-974 (2022)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A flat speckled skate stepping along a sandy ocean floor on its two rear fins, leaving small tracks in the sand.
image.caption: Little skates walk on pelvic fins wired by an ancient Hox and FoxP1 program shared with limb motor neurons.
